Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=attribution+of+causal+responsibility+in+path-dependent+autonomous+decision+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. The article's original contribution is the Temporal Anchor Convergence Standard (TACS), a three-part interpretive frameworkanchor declaration, divergence disclosure, and a default convergence-priority rule keyed to informational control over the intervening period-designed to make the divergence visible to courts and regulators rather than resolved silently by whichever doctrine a claimant happens to plead first. The article confronts the principal counterargument, that existing presumption-based reforms already solve the evidentiary problem regardless of which doctrinal anchor is used, and identifies the conditions under which that objection holds and the conditions under which it does not. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative rather than empirical, and its conclusions are correspondingly limited to the legal architecture of liability rather than to its practical enforcement rates, which remain largely undocumented.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.3967091\", \"title\": [\"Attribution of Collective Causal Responsibility to Individual Actors in Stochastic Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>We develop an attribution of collective causal responsibility to individual actors in stochastic nonlinear systems: we take an existing measure of collective causal responsibility from  Vallentyne (2008) and Baumgärtner (2020), introduce four elementary axioms on the attribution of collective responsibility to individuals, and propose a measure of individual causal responsibility that is uniquely implied by these axioms. Our approach is inspired by Shapley's (1953) fundamental concept of how to divide a collective effect into individual marginal contributions. The generic setting is a set of systems with potential regime shifts where actions affect the regime-shift probabilities -- e.g. technical systems, traffic systems, financial markets, managed ecosystems, or the Earth's climate system. This paper closes several gaps in the literature on responsibility attribution: our concept is intensive, has cardinal properties and allows for multiple actors with simultaneous actions. This is relevant for implementing efficient incentive schemes and liability for managers of stochastic systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3967091\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2021]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4212062\", \"title\": [\"A Theory of Causal Responsibility Attribution\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>People often act out of a desire to be responsible for good and not for bad events. Similarly, people frequently reward and punish other people if they perceive them to be responsible for the implementation of events that they like or dislike. When the implementation of an event depends on the interaction of multiple persons and, potentially, moves of nature, the determinants of such responsibility perceptions are not well understood. In this paper, I propose a notion of causal responsibility which attempts to objectively capture the causal importance of a person’s action for the implementation of an event in such situations. A laboratory experiment shows that the notion successfully predicts people’s responsibility perceptions. Furthermore, I incorporate the notion in a framework of responsibility preferences and study its implications for worker motivation and the design of voting rules. Finally, I show that the notion can explain experimentally elicited behavior and punishment and reward patterns in multi-agent situations that are not well-explained by existing social preference theories.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4212062\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/cved8911\", \"title\": [\"Forward-Looking and Backward-Looking Responsibility Attribution in Multi-Agent Sequential Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As AI systems gain more and more agency in modern-day society, the problem of responsibility attribution in AI is no longer just a philosophically interesting one, but a practical one as well. The rise of AI agency means that an increasing number of everyday tasks are now being handled by AI agents. As a result, addressing conceptual and technical challenges of attributing responsibility for the failure of a multi-agent AI system has become urgent. Such challenges are particularly prominent when the temporal dimension of decision making is taken into account. In general, the concept of responsibility attribution may have different meanings depending on the context. In particular, in my research I consider the distinction between forward-looking and backward-looking responsibility. Forward-looking responsibility looks at the future and holds agents accountable for what is expected to happen. On the other hand, backward-looking responsibility looks at the past and holds agents accountable for a specific realization of the system and an outcome of interest. This paper summarizes my contributions on forward- and backward-looking responsibility attribution in multi-agent sequential decision making and describes my future research plans.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/cved8911\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 5, 30]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "940ea18e971957c1878c173bcbcb8b4b76d9355754683b70c86a5c13880eb2d3", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7473639", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.3967091", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.4212062", "doi:10.65109/cved8911"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3967091", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4212062", "https://doi.org/10.65109/cved8911"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
